sections.text: Lord Shri Krishna said: Listen, O Arjuna! And I will tell thee how thou shalt know Me in my Full perfection, practising meditation with thy mind devoted to Me, and having Me for thy refuge.
I will reveal this knowledge unto thee, and how it may be realised; which, once accomplished, there remains nothing else worth having in this life.
Among thousands of men scarcely one strives for perfection, and even amongst those who gain occult powers, perchance but one knows me in truth.

Unlike a car with its users manual, we are born without instructions on how to live. We experience lifes vicissitudes without a so-called users manual. The Gita has been described as such a guide.
We have seen that the first six chapters described Jivatma, the conditioned self. The science which we are interested in is that of the self. What is the nature of my being? Thats the quest in learning Bhagavad Gita.
The self -- in Sanskrit, Atma -- is what Im trying to figure out. The first six chapters taught me what the conditioned self is called: Jivatma, what you and I call myself. This is me, this myself, this is yourself. That self is conditioned by my perception of who I am.
The I that refers to my body, my mind, my intellect, and all the things I have achieved -- thats Jivatma in Vedanta. It is nothing but a conditioned self. Conditioned by this body, mind, and intellect.
Just as room space is space, just like the space outside -- but I call it room space because its conditioned by the room. The room is made up of four walls, a floor, and a ceiling. If you take one of those away, its no longer a room, but the space itself remains.
Space was always here. I created the conditioning. Now I call it room space.
Similarly, I created the conditioning called me -- this body, this mind, this intellect -- and they called it Jiva Atma. Every conditioned being is a Jivatma. Who that is, we have discussed in detail in the first six chapters: who I am, how I act in this world, what the consequences of my actions are, and how I can avoid sorrow and unhappiness. Karma Yoga culminated in meditation -- what some may call Raja Yoga.
We started with Karma Yoga, then graduated to Dhyana Yoga, the yoga of meditation. Now we need to know: where do I go from here? I understood what Jivatma is. I need to now understand who Paramatma is.
Supreme self, space, room space, universal space -- I understood what the room space is, but my mind right now cant grasp what the universal space is. So I now need to graduate from room space to understanding the universal space. For that, I first start with understanding the conditioned self, the Jivatma, and then move toward the Paramatma, the supreme self.
The next six chapters will tell us about Ishvara, the Lord Almighty, who is the creator of this universe and who is in control of all the Jivatmas. All Jivatmas are functioning because of Ishwara, just as all room spaces in all the rooms in the world exist because of universal space. But right now I only understand the conditioned self.
From Jivatma, Im migrating to Paramatma. I may not understand Him in His essence, so I now need to come down to one level below -- to Him as the creator. Him as the controller of all the beings -- that is whom we call Ishvara.
My friends who know me may not know me as an architect, but my clients know me as one. They can only understand me through the relationship they have with me. I am the creation of the Creator.
If I can understand my relationship with Him -- the creation and the Creator -- thats easier than finding out who He is in all His entirety. So well start with Ishvara, the one who created this universe as I can perceive, feel, and touch it -- which is called Prakriti in Sanskrit. The one who is in control of the Prakriti is Purusha.
The next six chapters will explore that. And it has to culminate into devotion for that Paramatma. For me to know someone in his or her entirety, I need to identify with him or her.
That identification becomes love. For me to know Paramatma, I need to devote myself to Paramatma. I need to start identifying with that Paramatma.
That identification will become devotion. So these six chapters will culminate into 12th chapter Bhakti Yoga, the yoga of devotion. We started with Karma Yoga.
We graduated to Raja Yoga. Were now marching towards Bhakti Yoga, the yoga of devotion. So these first three verses -- Bhagavan, in the last verse of the previous chapter, set up the stage and said: the one who wants to know yoga, even out of just curiosity -- I really want to know what yoga is all about -- hes better than the Karma Kandi, the one who is simply doing rituals.
Im a very religious person. I need to have my business run properly by Bhagavans grace. Early morning, before I go to my job, I need to do the puja as quickly as I can.
Before 8 oclock, I do puja and run. Im done with Bhagavan today. Then I say, well, now things are getting even more hectic.
I actually asked somebody in India, and I said, What about puja? He said, I just go online and I have this website. You click on Ganpati Puja, the Ganpati Murti comes in, there is agarbatti on the side. You click on the agarbatti, it lights up.
You click on the lamp, the lamp lights up. You click on the garland, garland comes on. You click on the aarti -- I can do it anywhere now.
Its very, very easy. So we say thats Karmakanda -- just performing rituals mechanically. I decided that I have to do this to be on the good side of the Lord -- that is a Karma Kandi. Bhagavan said, even one who merely wants to know yoga is better than a Karma Kandi. I may not have any interest in performing yoga, but if I want to know what yoga is, Im at least better than that.
Then obviously, the yogi is said to be better than a Gnani, a Tapasvi, or even a Sanyasi. Because the yogi is the one who has given up everything in terms of the fruits of actions and is relying on the Lord to give him the Karma Phala. Ill do my duty as His vehicle. Im just a Nimitta Matra. My actions are there because Im empowered by the Lord to do this.
I can speak because Im alive. Im alive because the consciousness is still functioning through this body. That consciousness belongs to the Supreme Consciousness.
You and I are conscious of each other because the same consciousness functioning through me is functioning through you. If you had two incompatible programs, we wouldnt be talking to each other. Two computers dont talk to each other if one is on Windows and the other on a different system.
But we can, because the same consciousness is functioning through you and me. So Bhagawan said, the one who has given up his sense of I am in control and surrendered -- hes a yogi, and hes better than all of that. Now Bhagavan says Arjuna is all charged up and wants to know.
The seventh chapter continues as Gnana Vignana Yoga, the Yoga of Knowledge and Wisdom. So what is the difference? We obviously had a discussion last time. Something which I know is Gnana.
Something which I do not know is obviously ignorance. Then Vignana -- Visheshta Gnana -- is special knowledge. Normal knowledge is: I know you people are in the room.
Thats knowledge because I can see it and vouch for it. The knowledge which I can perceive, feel, and touch through my senses is Gnana. But when we process that knowledge and come to another conclusion, that is Vignana.
So the Chidananda Bhagavad Gita which I have here -- It basically says Gnana requires sight -- in other words, the senses. Vignana is insight. Gnana requires tuition: for me to learn Bhagavad Gita, I had to go to a qualified teacher. Sight requires tuition.
But the knowledge of what I learned requires intuition. Music is the one which I really understand well because I have a lot of difficulty learning that. I went to my teacher to learn that and he will say, Rajan, do this sargam.
You know, Subha says, its too difficult. I know how to sing song. I said, no, no, you need to do this sargam.
And while I was doing it, it was so difficult. And then he told me that one day it will come naturally to you and you yourself will understand how to do it. And I didnt believe him.
But it did happen exactly that way. Things which I couldnt learn while he was teaching me, but I know what to do came naturally to me. At one point, when I was trying to practice it, I didnt need to make any effort to figure out what it is -- because it became my own knowledge.
Intuitively, I knew what it was. I asked my nephew, who has been a prodigy since he was about six years old -- he can do any music he wants. I asked him, Advaita, teach me how to do this. He said, uncle, I dont know how to teach you.
I myself do not know how Im doing it. I just know how to do it. So the vignana is the intuitive knowledge.
Once you gather the knowledge and absorbed it as your own, intuitively you use it for its right application is vignana. So Bhagavan says, sometimes its translated as wisdom. Wisdom is not something you sit down and decide to do.
Wisdom is when somebody says something and you know what to do with it. Its an intuitive knowledge born out of the knowledge and experiences you have accumulated. And that wisdom you cannot claim as your own, because something in you has the ability to grasp that knowledge.
When youre alive, you can do it. When youre dead, you cant be conscious of it. Your consciousness is that entity which is the source of intuition.
So Bhagavan said, I will tell you now. Yogam yunjan, mad ashrayha, asansayam samagram mam, yatha jnasyasi tat shrunu. This is a promise to all beings who really want to know who they are. He said, Now listen carefully, O Partha, because Ill tell you what the knowledge and the wisdom is. But here are the prerequisites.
With your mind clinging to me, taking refuge in me, and practicing Yoga, you will without any doubt know me in full. Three things. Bhagavan said, Im going to tell you what you need to know, but your mind should be focused on me. If I want to learn something, I obviously need to be focused on that.
I want to find out how my BlackBerry works -- I need to be focused on it. I still cant use all the features on my BlackBerry because Im not focused enough.

Krishna opens this chapter with three prerequisites for knowing the Divine: a mind clinging to the Supreme (mayyasaktamanah), taking refuge in Him (madasrayah), and practicing yoga (yogam yunjan). Today, examine which of these three areas needs your attention most. Is your mind scattered across countless worldly concerns, rarely resting on the deeper questions of existence? Do you truly take refuge in a higher purpose, or do you rely solely on your own limited efforts? How consistent is your actual practice of meditation and self-inquiry?
Consider Krishnas sobering statement that among thousands of people, scarcely one strives for perfection, and even among those who strive, few truly know Him in essence. This is not meant to discourage but to inspire urgency. Ask yourself: Am I among those rare seekers who genuinely pursue self-knowledge, or am I content with surface-level spirituality? The distinction between Jnana (knowledge gained through study) and Vijnana (wisdom through direct realization) is crucial here. Today, take one teaching you intellectually understand and consciously apply it in a difficult situation. Notice the gap between knowing and being.
What would it mean to move from tuition to intuition in your spiritual life? Just as a musician eventually plays without conscious effort, how might you internalize these teachings so deeply that right understanding becomes spontaneous?
